o: Identify ethical, cultural, environmental and privacy effects of technology.
Explain who benefits or could be disadvantaged.
Develop a balanced judgement using a specific situation.
c: Ethical questions concern what is fair or responsible, even when an action is legal. Legal issues concern laws that apply. Consider the effect on different groups, not only technical capability.

Digital services make communication and collaboration easier, but unequal access to devices or reliable Internet creates a digital divide. Global digital communication can also affect language, culture and social interaction.
Electronic devices require energy and materials to produce, run and dispose of. Repair and recycling can reduce e-waste; increased energy demand has environmental costs.

Data collection may improve services but can expose personal information. Biased automated decisions or inaccessible technology can disadvantage people, so design should be fair, transparent and inclusive.

m.title: Online-only access · fair inclusion
m.q: A town library introduces an online-only booking service. Explain TWO ethical or social concerns that the library should consider. [4 marks]
st: Identify the users: some visitors may have no broadband or suitable device.
Online-only booking could exclude those without digital access [1], preventing them from booking services easily [1].
Some visitors may lack digital skills or accessible interfaces [1], creating barriers to fair use [1].
Two concerns and linked effects. The library could also provide an in-person/telephone option.

w: A health centre makes appointments mainly through a mobile app. Explain two ways this could affect different patients. [4 marks]

Patients who have smartphones can book appointments remotely [1], making access more convenient [1]. Patients without devices or with accessibility difficulties may be excluded [1], making healthcare harder to access [1].
A school replaces working tablets every two years. Explain an environmental concern and a possible mitigation. [4 marks]

Frequent replacement increases e-waste/material demand [1], creating disposal and manufacturing impacts [1]. Repair, reuse or recycle functioning tablets [1], reducing waste and demand for new materials [1].
An online service collects location data to recommend local events. Explain one benefit and one privacy risk. [4 marks]

Location data can enable more relevant nearby recommendations [1], helping users find suitable events [1]. Storing precise location histories [1] risks revealing where users visit if data is misused or exposed [1].

k.q: Ask a user whether they can access the online service, then show a suitable option.
k.code:
hasInternet = input("Internet access? yes/no")
if hasInternet == "yes" then
    print("Online booking available")
else
    print("Offer telephone booking")
endif
p: Predict the output for an input of yes.
Predict and test an input of no.
Change the two output messages to describe an alternative library-booking option.
k.a:
Input yes gives Online booking available. Input no gives Offer telephone booking.

Example adaptation:
hasInternet = input("Internet access? yes/no")
if hasInternet == "yes" then
    print("Use the online form")
else
    print("Book at the desk")
endif

This is a small simulation rather than a real booking system.

e:
State TWO environmental concerns linked to digital technology. [2 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official OCR past paper.
E-waste from discarded devices [1] and electricity/energy consumption [1]. Other clear valid concerns include manufacturing emissions or extracting raw materials.

A secondary school moves all homework online. Explain one benefit and one social disadvantage. [4 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official OCR past paper.

Homework can be accessed anywhere with Internet [1], making resources easy to distribute/submit [1]. Pupils without reliable devices or connectivity [1] may find it harder to complete work, widening inequality [1].

Evaluate how a council's move towards digital-only public services could affect citizens and the environment. [6 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official OCR past paper.

Digital services can reduce travel/paper use [1], improving convenience and possibly resource use [1]. They may exclude people without reliable devices/skills [1], creating an access barrier [1]. Data collection could compromise privacy [1] without suitable protections, so a justified balance including alternative access is important [1].
v: Judgements about what is fair, right or responsible.
Unequal access to digital devices, connectivity and skills.
Control and protection of information about individuals.
How technology affects customs, language or social interaction.
Effects on resources, energy, pollution and waste.
How readily people with different needs can use a service.
x: A service can be legal but still raise ethical concerns about fairness and access.
r: Name the utility that rearranges file blocks on a magnetic hard disk. [1 mark]
State the purpose of a device driver. [2 marks]
Software that enables an operating system to communicate [1] with a specific hardware device/peripheral [1].
State the difference between RAM and ROM in whether each retains data without power. [2 marks]
RAM is volatile and loses stored information when power is removed [1]; ROM is non-volatile [1].
A hotel has guest and manager accounts on one shared computer. Explain how user management prevents guests from changing booking records. [4 marks]
OS assigns different user accounts [1] and can authenticate the person signing in [1]. Access rights restrict guest permissions [1], so only authorised staff can edit booking records [1].

priorExam.q: A doctor encrypts confidential files on a portable drive. Explain TWO reasons this helps keep information private. [4 marks]
priorExam.a: Encryption transforms readable data into ciphertext [1], preventing straightforward reading [1]. A decryption key is needed [1], so losing the drive does not automatically expose readable records [1].
